topic: Which bird migrates the farthest? (Arctic tern)
policy_note: Every spoken or shown fact → a claim with ≥ 2 independent publishers; core claims need a primary/scholarly source.

pnas_egevang_2010.publisher: PNAS (Egevang, Stenhouse, Phillips, Petersen, Fox & Silk 2010)
pnas_egevang_2010.title: Tracking of Arctic terns Sterna paradisaea reveals longest animal migration
pnas_egevang_2010.notes: 11 terns from Greenland (n=10) and Iceland (n=1) with 1.4-g geolocators; mean annual round trip ≈ 70,900 km (some > 80,000 km); North Atlantic stopover 41–53°N 27–41°W; southbound along West Africa (7 birds) or Brazil (4); all returned on a sigmoidal mid-Atlantic track; wintered south of 58°S, 0–61°W (Weddell Sea sector); species < 125 g

wiki_arctic_tern.title: Arctic tern
wiki_arctic_tern.notes: average annual round trip about 70,900 km for Iceland/Greenland birds; lives about 30 years → some 2.4 million km in a lifetime, 'a roundtrip from Earth to the Moon more than three times'; weight 86–127 g; sees two summers a year

britannica_arctic_tern.title: Arctic tern
britannica_arctic_tern.notes: breeds in the Arctic and winters in Antarctic waters; the longest migration of any bird

audubon_arctic_tern.title: Arctic Tern — Guide to North American Birds
audubon_arctic_tern.notes: champion long-distance migrant; Arctic breeding grounds to Antarctic pack ice; tracked individuals cover ~70,000 km a year

wiki_godwit.title: Bar-tailed godwit
wiki_godwit.notes: Alaska → New Zealand flight is the longest known NON-STOP flight of any bird; round trip over 29,000 km — far shorter than the tern's annual total

nasa_moon.title: Moon facts — average distance 384,400 km
nasa_moon.notes: mean Earth–Moon distance 384,400 km; 3 round trips ≈ 2.31 million km (checks the 'three Moon round trips' framing)

claims.text: The Arctic tern has the longest known migration of any animal: tracked Greenland/Iceland birds averaged about 70,900 km a year between Arctic breeding grounds and the Antarctic (Weddell Sea sector).
vo: pole to pole, about seventy-one thousand kilometres a year

claims.text: Egevang et al. (2010) tracked 11 terns with geolocators: southbound along the West African (or Brazilian) coast, with a North Atlantic stopover; all returned on a sigmoidal track up the mid-Atlantic.
vo: trackers on greenland terns traced it

claims.text: Over a ~30-year life an Arctic tern flies some 2.4 million km — more than three round trips to the Moon (384,400 km each way).
vo: over a thirty-year life, that's two point four million kilometres

claims.text: An Arctic tern weighs 86–127 g (PNAS: < 125 g) — lighter than a typical 100–150 g bar of soap.
vo: on a bird lighter than a bar of soap

myths.myth: The bar-tailed godwit migrates the farthest.
myths.reality: The godwit holds the longest NON-STOP flight (Alaska → New Zealand); its round trip is ~29,000 km. The Arctic tern's yearly total is more than double.

myths.myth: Arctic terns fly about 40,000 km a year.
myths.reality: That was the pre-tracking estimate; geolocators showed ~70,900 km on average.

guardrails.why: Contested name — say 'the Gulf' or use both names (docs/BORDER_POLICY.md).
Sovereignty language on disputed areas is banned; say administers / claims.

landscape.our_gap: Feed versions show a stock tern over 'Arctic tern — 70,000 km'. Nobody draws the published loop (Africa down, mid-Atlantic up) or ties the Moon comparison to the real distance.
